summary.title: bliki: Technical Debt
summary.one_liner: Technical debt is a metaphor for the cost of internal code quality problems (cruft): the extra effort per change is the interest, and refactoring is paying down the principal.
keywords: is taking on technical debt bad
takeaways: Cruft is deficiency in internal quality that makes changing software harder; the extra effort per feature is the interest on that debt.
Cleaning up cruft pays off only when enough future changes will benefit, so refactoring is worth it in areas you modify often.
Pay down the principal gradually, tackling the code you touch most, rather than in one large cleanup.
Crufty code that is rarely modified can be left alone; high-activity areas need a zero-tolerance attitude to cruft.
Using debt to justify neglecting quality often backfires, because teams hit the design payoff line quickly and deliver slower.
summary.summary: Martin Fowler's bliki entry explains technical debt as a metaphor coined by Ward Cunningham for the consequences of software cruft, where extra effort to add features is the interest and cleanup is paying the principal. He uses a worked example (four days versus six days, with a five-day cleanup that pays off over multiple features) to show why gradual cleanup in frequently changed code is usually the best route. The article also covers where the metaphor breaks down, the risks of taking on debt to justify neglecting quality, and links to the Technical Debt Quadrant and further reading. Fowler revised it in April 2019 from a 2003 original.
